hook.text: One shark attack makes national news. Suddenly everyone thinks sharks are a top killer.

buildup.text: An availability cascade starts with a dramatic event. Media covers it, people discuss it, media covers it more.

discovery.text: Repetition creates perceived truth. A risk mentioned often enough feels common even when data says it is rare.

twist.text: Policy follows. Billions are spent on terrorism prevention while heart disease, a far bigger killer, is underfunded.

climax.text: When a risk feels huge, check the actual numbers. Dramatic does not mean frequent. Media distorts probability.

punchline.text: What you hear most is rarely what kills most.

quiz.question: What drives an availability cascade?
options: Media repetition making rare events feel common

details.summary: An availability cascade traps decision-makers by creating a self-reinforcing cycle where repeated discussion of a risk makes it seem increasingly urgent, driving disproportionate responses to newly salient threats while genuinely important risks are neglected.
details.whyItMatters: Decision-makers allocate resources based on what feels most urgent, which is shaped by availability rather than actual severity.
takeaways: Repeated discussion inflates perceived urgency beyond actual risk levels
Media amplification makes some risks dominate decision agendas disproportionately
Base rate analysis helps distinguish genuine urgency from availability inflation

faq.question: How do you avoid falling into an availability cascade trap?
faq.answer: Anchor decisions on statistical base rates rather than recent salience. Ask whether the risk changed or just the discussion about it. Track how your risk priorities shift over time and compare to objective data rather than media coverage.

faq.question: Can availability cascades affect corporate strategy?
faq.answer: Absolutely. A competitor's highly publicized failure can cause an industry-wide overreaction. A viral social media complaint can redirect an entire quality program. The key is distinguishing signal from amplified noise in the information environment.
